newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodians get first glimpse of footage of Pol Pot.
newsitem.headline: Cambodians get first glimpse of footage of Pol Pot.

text.p: Cambodians got their first glimpse of footage of reviled Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot on Tuesday and many people were surprised that the man responsible for the death of more than one million of their compatriots was so old and frail.

ABC-TV of the United States, which has exclusive footage of last week's "trial" of Pol Pot, showed the video in Phnom Penh's central market and near Wat Phnom, a main temple and popular meeting place.
Hundreds of Cambodians crowded around a small television screen to catch a glimpse of the man not seen by outsiders since late 1979.
"People were surprised to see him so old and using a cane," said one witness.
"Others were happy to see him caught, but wary that this could be another political game of the Khmer Rouge. They want to see him brought before a real court in Phnom Penh first."
A member of the ABC team said that in general the reaction of those seeing the video was more subdued than expected.
"It wasn't the reaction they wanted, the people were more curious than anything else," the crew member said.

Nate Thayer, a correspondent with the Far Eastern Economic Review, was the first reporter to see Pol Pot in 18 years when he witnessed the rebel leader's denunciation and sentencing to life in detention at a show trial in the Khmer Rouge's Anlong Veng base in the north of country.
Thayer sold video tape of the trial to ABC.
Pol Pot was the architect of the Khmer Rouge's "killing fields" rule from 1975-79 during which more than a million Cambodians were killed by execution, torture, disease, starvation or hard labour.
As some Cambodians were getting their first glimpse of Pol Pot a shrine dedicated to his countless victims was deserted just a few km (miles) away.
The shrine at Choeng Ek, a former Khmer Rouge execution site, was built by the Hanoi-backed government which replaced the Khmer Rouge and is one of the capital's tourist sites.
Hundreds of skulls, unearthed from nearby mass graves, are stacked high in the shrine on the outskirts of Phnom Penh.
But on a rainy Tuesday afternoon the only visitors to the grim site were a Reuters reporter and photographer.
"Before the fighting on July 5 and 6 we got many tourists but now we get only one or two day," said a caretaker at the Choeng Ek memorial.
Second Prime Minister Hun Sen ousted First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh after two days of battles in Phnom Penh during that time.
"Do you think there will ever be peace in Cambodia or more terrible fighting?" the caretaker asked.

Khmer Rouge radio first denounced Pol Pot, now almost 70, in mid-June, shortly after a bloody split in the secretive Maoist group's top leadership in which defence chief Son Sen and almost a dozen members of his family were slaughtered.
Pol Pot and three of his commanders were found guilty of murdering Son Sen and his family, of "destroying national reconciliation" and of stealing money from the party, Thayer said.
The three "drunk and corrupt" commanders were also said to have raped the wives of their comrades, he said.
But in Phnom Penh, strongman Hun Sen said on Monday that Pol Pot was still in charge of the rebel group and was playing a political game.
"It is a political game of the Khmer Rouge. Pol Pot is in Anlong Veng. He is the leader of the Khmer Rouge forces," Hun Sen said.
